youtube.baslik: Case: The Dissatisfied Hearing Aid User | Lesson 280 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
In a fictional case, we analyze the complaint of a dissatisfied hearing aid user in a structured way: physical checks and the listening stethoscope, data logging, real-ear measurement at high input levels, fine-tuning from the user's words to settings, understanding in noise and the QuickSIN, realistic expectations counseling and follow-up.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Dillon, Hearing Aids; Killion et al., QuickSIN (2004); Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology; ASHA, Hearing Aids for Adults.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

sahneler.alt: A structured approach from complaint to solution
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we work step by step through the complaint of a dissatisfied user who leaves their hearing aids in a drawer.
We will cover structured analysis of the complaint, data logging, fine-tuning and realistic expectations counseling.

maddeler.metin: Bilateral hearing aids for four months
Hearing aids in a drawer most days

cumleler: Our case is fictional: a sixty-six-year-old person got bilateral behind-the-ear hearing aids four months ago.
They missed the follow-up visit; now, at their spouse's insistence, they come in saying these hearing aids do not work.
The main complaint is not understanding conversation at all in crowded, noisy places.
They also say the sound of cutlery and some speakers' voices seems metallic and tinny.
So they do not wear the hearing aids most days and leave them in a drawer.
As we will soon see, the user's own words carry valuable clues to the source of the problem.
A structured approach starts with listening; the complaint is recorded in the person's own words, just as it is said.
Then we ask in which settings, with which sounds and since when the complaint occurs.
Next comes measurement: the data log is read, the device is checked physically and real-ear measurement is repeated.
Adjustments follow the findings; when possible, one change is made at a time so its effect can be understood.
Finally, at the next visit, the person is asked whether the change helped.
This order gets results much faster than changing settings at random.
Every complaint visit starts with otoscopy; in this case the ear canals are clear, with no significant earwax.
Domes and receivers are in place; there is no redness or pressure mark in the ear canal.
Listening with a stethoscope, the right hearing aid sounds clear, while the left is clearly weak and muffled.
The left receiver's wax filter is blocked; when the filter is changed, the sound returns to normal.
A simple maintenance problem may have made the person hear weakly and unevenly between the two ears.
Charge status, clean microphone ports and correct program function are also reviewed in the same check.
The audiogram shows a symmetric sensorineural loss in both ears, sloping toward the high frequencies.
Bone conduction overlaps air conduction; tympanograms are type A in both ears.
Compared with the test before fitting, thresholds show no significant change.
So there is no new hearing loss to explain the complaint; we look for the problem in the device, settings and use.
If hearing had worsened suddenly or markedly, referral to a physician would be needed before any adjustment.
Data logging shows how many hours a day, and in which settings, the device was used.
For this person, average daily use is only an hour and a half; so the brain had no chance to get used to hearing with the devices.
About half of the use time was in noisy speech settings; so the device was used most in the hardest setting.
The log also shows the person often turned the volume down; this suggests loud sounds were uncomfortable.
The log is not a tool for blame; it is looked at together with the person, and they are asked why they used the devices so little.
The person says they wore the hearing aids only at crowded gatherings, and got the worst results there.
Real-ear measurement is repeated with speech-like signals at average and high levels.
For average speech, the measurement is near target; there seems to be no problem here.
But for high-level input, output above two thousand hertz is clearly above target.
A description of sound as metallic and tinny is often linked to too much high-frequency output at high input levels.
This finding also explains why the person often turned the volume down.
The adjustment goal is clear: reduce high-frequency gain only for high inputs, while keeping soft and average sounds.

ogeler.metin: Too much treble at high input

cumleler: The first step of fine-tuning is working out which acoustic problem the person's words point to.
A description of sound as muffled or far away often suggests too little high-frequency gain.
Hearing one's own voice as if talking inside a bucket suggests the occlusion effect or too much low-frequency gain.
Not understanding in noise is not always a settings problem; program, microphones and expectations are considered together.
These pairings are a starting point; decisions are made with measurement and with the person.
In our case, the description and the real-ear measurement point the same way: too much treble at high input levels.

maddeler.metin: Treble gain reduced at high input

cumleler: The first change is already done: the blocked filter in the left device was replaced, and the person was shown how to change it.
High-frequency gain was reduced for high input levels; audibility for soft and average inputs was kept.
A separate program with directional microphones and noise reduction active was added for crowded places.
After the change, real-ear measurement was repeated, and a recorded everyday sound scene was played with the person.
An all-day wearing plan was made, starting at home and in quiet places; crowded gatherings will be the next step.

maddeler.metin: Turning up volume doesn't change SNR

cumleler: For understanding in noise, the Quick Speech-in-Noise test, or QuickSIN, is done; the signal-to-noise ratio, or SNR, loss is nine decibels.
According to the test manual, this is a moderate SNR loss.
So to understand in noise, the person needs a higher signal-to-noise ratio, or SNR, than people with normal hearing.
Raising both speech and noise together does not change the ratio; so turning up the volume is not a solution on its own.
Directional microphones, and a remote microphone placed on the table, can improve the ratio by separating the talker's voice from the noise.
Strategies such as sitting with one's back to the noise source and facing the talker are also explained.

maddeler.metin: Hearing aids _do not restore normal_ hearing
Some difficulty in noise may remain

cumleler: Expectations are discussed openly: hearing aids do not restore normal hearing, but they improve audibility and understanding.
The person is told in advance that some difficulty in noisy places will remain; knowing this reduces disappointment.
We explain that the brain may take weeks to adjust to sounds, and that regular use speeds up the process.
Together we rewrite the Client Oriented Scale of Improvement, or COSI, goals concretely; for example, dinner talk with the spouse.
Expectations counseling is not a one-time talk, but a process continued at every follow-up.

sahneler.metin: Before adjusting, listen to the device, read the data log, and write down the complaint in the person's own words.
cumleler: A tip from the field: before opening the software, listen to the device with a listening stethoscope and check the ear canal.
A blocked filter or a wrongly fitted dome can have a bigger effect than the most complex adjustment.
Write the complaint in the person's own words; "plates in the kitchen are piercing" tells you far more than "sounds bother me."
Record every change and its reason in the file; only then can you know at the next visit what worked.
At the six-week follow-up, the data log shows an average of seven hours a day.
The person says the metallic sound has largely gone and they now rarely turn the volume down.
They rate the goal of talking with their spouse at dinner as much better.
At crowded gatherings it is slightly better; they decide to try the remote microphone option.
Most of the dissatisfaction came not from the device itself, but from maintenance, settings, use and expectations.
At the next follow-up, the effect of the noise program and the remote microphone will be reassessed.
First, the complaint is written in the file in the person's own words.
Then the findings: the data log, the device's physical condition and the real-ear measurement results.
Every change and its rationale is written, including the reason for any deliberate departure from target.
What was discussed in expectations counseling, the rewritten goals and the plan for the next visit are added.
This record keeps the process continuous when another colleague sees the person.

maddeler.metin: Device and ear first: filter, dome, wax
Data log and REM guide adjustment

cumleler: With dissatisfaction, the complaint is heard in the person's words, structured by setting and sound, and confirmed by measurement.
Before adjusting, the ear canal and device are checked; simple problems like a blocked filter are common.
The data log and real-ear measurement show which way fine-tuning should go.
Realistic expectations counseling and planned follow-up keep the user from giving up on the hearing aids.

sahneler.soru: Sounds seem metallic. Most likely cause?
secenekler: Too much treble at high input
sahneler.aciklama: A metallic, tinny description is often linked to too much _high-frequency output at high input levels_.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: the user hears cutlery as metallic and tinny. Which possibility comes to mind first?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: too much high-frequency output at high input levels.
This is confirmed by real-ear measurement; high-frequency gain is reduced only for high inputs, while soft sounds are kept.
